messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rahul, a 52-year-old HVAC technician of South Eastern Asian descent, had been working on a construction site when disaster struck. A leak in one of the chemical storage tanks released a toxic cloud that enveloped him and several coworkers. Rahul remembered the searing pain in his eyes and lungs, the sound of panicked screams, and the feeling of being unable to escape. As he stumbled out into fresh air, he saw one of his colleagues collapse, never to get up again. The incident left an indelible mark on Rahul's psyche. Even when others assured him that the site was safe now, even when his wife, Nalini, tried to comfort him at home, he couldn't shake off the feeling of perpetual danger. His body remained tense and ready to react, always poised for flight or fight. "I just can't trust it," Rahul would tell himself, his mind racing with worst-case scenarios whenever someone said he was safe. This persistent sense of threat began to dictate his daily life. Rahul started avoiding anything that could be stressful – he stopped taking on new projects at work and turned down social invitations from friends and family. "What if I get overwhelmed?" he would think, envisioning himself losing control in a crowded room or under pressure on the job site. He also became increasingly uncomfortable with being alone, whether it was in his workshop or even in their home when Nalini went out for errands. His mind would start racing with catastrophic thoughts – "What if someone breaks in?" or "What if there's another accident?" To mitigate these fears, Rahul developed an exhausting routine of checking doors and windows multiple times a day. As time passed, the habits he formed to cope with his perceived danger became ingrained. Rahul avoided relaxing altogether because it felt like letting his guard down. He couldn't bear the thought of being off-guard, even for a moment. His wife noticed that he never seemed to unwind anymore – no more lazy Sundays watching cricket or playing guitar as he used to. "I'm just too tired," Rahul would say, though Nalini knew it was more than exhaustion. One day, after months of struggling with his ever-present anxiety and increasingly erratic behavior, Rahul's wife sat him down for a heart-to-heart talk. She expressed her concerns about the toll this was taking on their relationship and his overall well-being. For the first time, Rahul realized he wasn't just living in fear – he was also losing himself to it. The thought sent a jolt of recognition through him: he needed help. That's when Rahul finally reached out for professional support, hoping to break free from this suffocating cycle of threat and avoidance that had taken over his life. As he sat in the therapist's office, recounting his story and the fears that now defined him, Rahul couldn't shake off the feeling that he was still trapped – waiting for the next disaster to strike, unsure if he'd ever be able to trust safety again.
